title: Other people's faults (244–255)
hookLine: others' faults are easy to see, our own hard; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own (Dhammapada 252)

lines: A RED PEN ON SOMEONE ELSE'S ESSAY.
A BLIND SPOT THE SIZE OF A TRUCK.
cards: Hand someone a stranger's essay and a red pen, and the mistakes leap off the page: a clumsy sentence here, a missing word there. Hand them their own essay, and the same mistakes go invisible.
Or listen to a friend describe her sister, every flaw laid out in perfect detail. Ask for her own three biggest flaws, and there's a long pause.
A perfect view of other people, and a blind spot the size of a truck about ourselves. Chapter eighteen names it exactly.

teach.b: Verse two fifty-two, in Max Müller's translation: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler."
Two pictures in one verse. First, winnowing: at harvest, farmers tossed grain into the wind so the light chaff would blow away.
Picture someone tossing another person's faults high into the air, scattering them across the whole village.

teach.h: THE CHEAT HIDES THE BAD DIE.
teach.b: Second, a cheat at dice, hiding the bad die so no one notices it. That's what we do with our own. The Pali word for fault here is vajja, something to be avoided, something blameworthy.

The next verse warns what happens to the fault-finder. Verse two fifty-three: "If a man looks after the faults of others, and is always inclined to be offended, his own passions will grow". The irony is sharp.
Constant judging doesn't make you better.
It feeds the very things you're judging.
Just before these lines, verse two fifty-one gives four more pictures: "There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed."
Then the chapter closes with a reminder that a person isn't made holy by outward show, which is where tomorrow's chapter picks up. None of this says other people have no faults.
It says the eye that sees theirs so clearly would do its best work turned around.

how: Buddhist monastics regularly confess their own faults to one another, and teachers often cite verse 252 to turn attention from criticizing others to examining oneself.

o: a harsh word that points out someone's flaw
a flaw you were born with and can't change
a fault, something blameworthy to avoid

games.q: match each image to its meaning.

s: the verse says other people have no faults
it says theirs are easy to see and ours are hard: turn the eye around.
verse 253 says constant fault-finding makes your own passions grow
in verse 251, the torrent is greed

games.q: a coworker keeps interrupting in meetings, and you've noticed every single time. what would verse 252 have you look at?
o: keep a list of every interruption.
whether you have a fault you're hiding like a bad die.
games.why: others' faults are easy to winnow in the wind; our own we hide "as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler."

practice: Think of someone whose faults you know by heart, name one silently, and gently turn the same bright light around: is there any trace of it in you?
Not to punish yourself, just to look, the way you'd check your own mirror; often there's a small echo, and if there isn't, look for the fault you'd least like anyone to see.
When you've seen it, oh, there it is, set it down and let the breath be plain and open.

wordCard.voice: Vajja. A fault, something blameworthy: verse two fifty-two says others' faults are easy to see, while our own are hard to see; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own.

orig.note: Pali: a fault, something to be avoided — sudassaṃ vajjam aññesaṃ, others' faults are easy to see.

carryVoice: Your line: easy to see others. Hard to see ourselves. Day two hundred six, done.
